For truth-table questions, write the rows in the order TT, TF, FT, FF and use the correct truth rule for each operator.
For a conditional, remember that it is false only when the antecedent is true and the consequent is false.
For an algebraic proof, start with L.H.S, show each expansion or algebraic rule clearly, and finish with “= R.H.S”, “⇒ L.H.S = R.H.S” and “Hence proved.”

explain.title: 1. A mathematical statement
explain.body: A sentence or mathematical expression which may be true or false but not both is called a statement. For example, 3 + 4 = 8 is a statement, and it is false.

explain.title: 2. Negation, conjunction and disjunction
explain.body: The negation ~p means “not p”. The conjunction p ∧ q means “p and q” and is true only when both statements are true. The disjunction p ∨ q means “p or q” and is true when at least one statement is true.

explain.title: 3. Conditional and biconditional
explain.body: A conditional has the form p → q, read “if p then q”. It is false only when p is true and q is false. A biconditional p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value.

explain.title: 4. Theorem, conjecture and axiom
explain.body: A theorem is a mathematical statement that has been proved true based on previously known facts. A conjecture is believed to be true based on observations but has not yet been proved. An axiom is a mathematical statement that we believe to be true without any evidence or requiring any proof.

explain.title: 5. How to prove an algebraic identity
explain.body: Start from L.H.S, use definitions and algebraic laws to simplify one step at a time, and show that the result is R.H.S. For odd integers, use x = 2k + 1 for some k ∈ Z; for even integers, use x = 2k for some k ∈ Z.

mistakes: Calling a conjecture a theorem before it has been proved.
Forgetting that a conjunction is true only when both statements are true.
Saying a conditional is false whenever its consequent is false; it is false only when the antecedent is also true.
Writing the converse instead of the contrapositive. The contrapositive reverses the order and negates both parts.
In a proof, skipping the algebraic steps or failing to state that the result equals R.H.S.
In an odd/even proof, not stating that the new integer parameter is an integer.

notes.title: Statements, logic and proof
notes.answer: A mathematical statement is a sentence or expression which may be true or false but not both. A proof is a logical sequence of steps that gives evidence that a statement is correct.
notes.explanation: A mathematical statement is a sentence or expression that is either true or false, but not both. A proof is a logical sequence of steps that gives evidence that a mathematical statement is correct.
notes.simple: A statement is something that can be true or false. A proof shows, step by step, why a mathematical statement is true.
examples: 3 + 4 = 8 is a mathematical statement; it is false.
If x is odd, write x = 2k + 1 for some k ∈ Z. Then x² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, so x² is odd.
steps: Use known definitions, facts or rules.
Write each logical or algebraic step clearly.
Show that the steps establish the claim.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the difference between a mathematical statement and its proof?
notes.checkAnswer: A statement is the claim; a proof is the logical evidence that establishes whether the claim is correct.

quiz.stem: Which of the following expressions is often related to inductive reasoning?
options: Statement is proven by a theorem
rationales: Correct: inductive reasoning draws general conclusions from observations or repeated experiments.
This describes a biconditional, not inductive reasoning.
This does not describe induction; induction uses observations to reach a general conclusion.
Reasoning from general principles is associated with deduction.

quiz.stem: Which of the following sentences describe deductive reasoning?
options: general conclusions from a limited number of observations
based on units of information that are accurate
rationales: This describes induction: drawing a general conclusion from observations.
Repeated experiments are associated with inductive reasoning.
This describes a mathematical statement, not deductive reasoning.
Correct: deduction draws conclusions from premises or well-known facts.

quiz.stem: Which one of the following statements is true?
options: The set of integers is finite
The sum of the interior angles of any quadrilateral is always 180°
All isosceles triangles are equilateral triangles
rationales: This is false because the set of integers is infinite.
This is false because the interior angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360°.
Correct: 22/7 is rational, so it is not an irrational number.
This is false because an isosceles triangle need not be equilateral.

quiz.stem: Which of the following statements is the best to represent the negation of the statement "The stove is burning"?
options: the stove is turned to low heat
it is both burning and not burning.
rationales: Correct: this directly states that the original statement is not true.
A dim stove might still be burning, so this is not its negation.
A stove on low heat could still be burning, so this is not its negation.
A statement and its negation cannot both be true; this does not express the negation correctly.

quiz.stem: The conjunction of two statements p and q is true when:
options: both p and q are false.
both p and q are true.
rationales: A conjunction is false when both statements are false.
Correct: p ∧ q is true only when both p and q are true.
If only q is true, the conjunction is false.
If only p is true, the conjunction is false.

quiz.stem: A conditional is regarded as false only when:
options: antecedent is true and consequent is false.
consequent is true and antecedent is false.
rationales: Correct: a conditional is false exactly when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false.
In this case the conditional is true.
The consequent may also be true, so this condition alone does not make it false.
The antecedent may be false, so this condition alone does not make it false.

quiz.stem: The statement “Every integer greater than 2 is a sum of two prime numbers” is:
rationales: It has not been proved in the section, so it is not a theorem.
Correct: it is presented as an unproved statement believed to be true, that is, a conjecture.
It is not accepted as a starting fact without proof; it is an unproved conjecture.
A postulate is an accepted statement without proof, often associated with geometry.

quiz.stem: The statement "A straight line can be drawn between any two points" is :
rationales: A theorem is proved from known facts, while this is accepted without proof.
A conjecture is believed true but remains unproved; this statement is given as an axiom.
Correct: the section lists this as a Euclid axiom.
Logic is a method of reasoning, not the name for this accepted geometric fact.

quiz.stem: The statement "The sum of the interior angle of a triangle is 180°” is:
rationales: A converse reverses the parts of a conditional; this statement is not presented in that form.
Correct: the statement is a mathematical result that can be proved, so it is a theorem.
The section gives it as an example of a true mathematical statement and theorem, not an axiom.
A conditional has an if-then form, which this statement does not have.
